extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in scientific machine learning, computational scientists, and applied mathematicians working on physics-informed neural networks (PINNs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for building, training, and analyzing physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to solve forward and inverse PDE problems, including architectural choices, loss design, training strategies, and theoretical/convergence considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss composition (PDE residual, boundary/initial conditions, data)
rubrics_metrics.description: PINN loss functions include terms reflecting the PDE residual (LF), the initial and boundary conditions (LB), and any observed data (Ldata); the overall loss is a weighted sum θ* = arg min_θ (ωF LF(θ) + ωB LB(θ) + ωd Ldata(θ)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly construct loss terms for equation residuals at collocation points, for boundary/initial conditions, and for data-fitting; choose and tune weights ωF, ωB, ωd to balance contributions. The paper emphasizes this composition as the fundamental design choice for PINNs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss term weighting and balancing
rubrics_metrics.description: Weights ωF, ωB, ωd must be selected to balance the magnitude and learning dynamics of the PDE, boundary, and data losses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imbalanced losses can prevent learning (e.g., PDE residual dominates and BCs/data ignored). Use adaptive weighting strategies, gradient-based balancing, or curriculum schedules to mitigate competing loss objectives. Monitor individual loss components during training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary condition enforcement: soft vs hard
rubrics_metrics.description: Boundary/initial conditions may be enforced softly via loss terms (soft BC) or hard-encoded into the network architecture (hard BC/PCNN).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soft BCs are flexible and straightforward but require proper loss weighting; hard BCs (custom architectures, multiplicative factors) enforce constraints exactly and can improve stability for some problems. Choose based on problem requirements (e.g., strict conservation or geometric constraints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Neural network architecture selection (FFNN, CNN, RNN, GAN, DeepONet, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: PINNs can use a variety of network architectures—feed-forward (MLP), convolutional (CNN), recurrent (RNN/LSTM/GRU), autoencoders, GANs, DeepONet, branch/trunk splits—chosen according to problem structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use FFNNs for general PDEs and smooth fields; CNNs/encoder–decoders for image-like or grid-structured data; RNNs or time-stepping cells for temporal integration or sequence modeling; DeepONet or multiple networks for operator learning or multi-output problems. Match architecture to data modality and geometric regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network depth and width (size/hyperparameters)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of layers and neurons per layer affects expressive power and trainability; small networks may underfit, very large networks may be hard to train, especially with limited data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirically choose depth/width for the PDE at hand (examples: 4–9 layers, 20–250 neurons used in literature). Consider problem complexity: discontinuities/shocks may require deeper networks or domain decomposition. Monitor training and test errors; consider capacity vs optimization trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple networks / domain decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Using multiple neural networks (one per subdomain, variable, or equation component) can improve expressivity and handle complex or multi-physics problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include separate networks for subdomains, for interfaces in Stefan problems, or branch/trunk DeepONet architectures. Domain decomposition helps with discontinuities and localized features; coordinate synchronization or interface conditions must be enforced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activation function choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Activation functions (tanh, sigmoid, ReLU, Swish, periodic functions) significantly affect PINN training; smooth activations are often preferred because PINNs require derivatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use infinitely differentiable activations (tanh, sigmoid, Swish) when high-order derivatives are computed (PINNs often need second derivatives). ReLU may hamper second-derivative evaluation. Trainable activations (Swish with parameter β) can improve convergence. Consider periodic/sinusoidal activations for problems with oscillatory solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic differentiation vs numerical differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: PINNs typically use automatic differentiation (AD) to compute PDE residual derivatives; older approaches used finite differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AD yields exact derivatives up to machine precision and integrates smoothly with modern frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch). Finite-difference approximations may be used with CNN-based discretizations but can introduce discretization error. Prefer AD unless specific numerical stencil approaches are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling of collocation points
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of collocation points (where the PDE residual is evaluated) matters: uniform grids, random sampling, Latin hypercube, or adaptive/residual-based sampling are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random or quasi-random sampling can avoid bias; adaptive/residual-based sampling focuses points where residual is large and can improve accuracy. Volume vs boundary point counts must be considered; sampling affects numerical conditioning and convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptive/residual-based refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Iteratively adapt collocation point distribution or network capacity based on residuals to improve solution in regions with large error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use residual-guided sampling, hp-refinement, or adaptive weighting to focus learning on difficult regions (steep gradients, shocks). hp-VPINN and similar methods implement domain/subdomain adaptive strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization and nondimensionalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Rescale PDEs and inputs/outputs (e.g., to [0,1]) to improve training stability and make activation regimes appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rescale variables to avoid wide dynamic ranges; dimensionless PDEs can avoid numerical ill-conditioning. Many activation functions behave best in limited input ranges; normalization of inputs and outputs is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimizer selection and training schedules
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of optimizer (Adam, L-BFGS, hybrid schemes) and learning rate schedules impacts convergence; common practice uses Adam for initial training then quasi-Newton (L-BFGS) for refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stochastic optimizers for large-scale problems or noisy data; L-BFGS can converge to lower loss for smaller problems. Combine Adam with later L-BFGS; tune learning rates and consider adaptive schedules, early stopping, and multi-stage training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initialization and its effect (NTK perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weight initialization influences training dynamics and can be analyzed through neural tangent kernel (NTK) perspectives; poor initialization may hamper convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established initialization schemes; be aware of NTK-related failure modes (when PINNs fail to train). Pretraining or transfer learning can provide better starting points for optimization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradient pathologies and mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: PINNs can suffer from problematic gradient flow (vanishing/exploding gradients, imbalance across loss terms, temporal stiffness), which prevents training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigate via adaptive loss weighting, gradient normalization, respecting causality (causal training), reordering/weighting collocation points, curriculum learning (time-wise), or reformulating loss (e.g., Sobolev or energy norms). Monitor gradients per loss component and apply remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causality and training order for time-dependent problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Respecting causality (temporal ordering) during training can improve convergence and avoid learning failures in time-dependent PDEs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use curriculum or causality-aware sampling (train from earlier times outward) and time-marching/discrete-step PINN variants. Methods that enforce causality can stabilize training for long-time integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variational / energy-based formulations (Deep Ritz, VPINN, hp-VPINN)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative PINN variants use variational/energy formulations where the loss is an energy functional rather than pointwise residuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deep Ritz and VPINN can be more appropriate when the PDE has an underlying variational principle; variational forms may yield better stability and convergence for certain PDE classes. Employ hp-VPINN for hp-refinement in a variational framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation and structure-preserving enforcement (CPINN, conservative forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcing conservation laws or conservative forms explicitly (e.g., CPINN) helps preserve physical invariants and improve solution fidelity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate residuals or architecture to ensure conserved quantities (mass, momentum, energy). Conservative enforcement is important in fluid dynamics, shocks, and advection-dominated problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling complex geometries and grids (coordinate transforms, PhyGeoNet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Irregular domains and non-uniform meshes challenge standard PINNs; coordinate transformations or geometry-adaptive CNNs (PhyGeoNet) can be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map irregular physical domains to reference domains, use geometry-aware architectures, or employ mesh-based CNN convolutions with appropriate padding representing boundary conditions. For complex geometries, hard enforcement of BCs or domain decomposition may help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discontinuities and shocks handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems with discontinuous solutions (shocks) are difficult for global smooth approximators; strategies include domain decomposition, multiple networks, hp-refinement, or specialized architectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple subdomain networks, increase network capacity in affected regions, or employ conservative formulations and adaptive sampling. Avoid expecting a single smooth FFNN to resolve steep discontinuities without targeted tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty quantification (Bayesian PINNs, adversarial UQ, ensembles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty in predictions using Bayesian PINNs, ensembles, adversarial methods, or probabilistic frameworks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ Bayesian neural networks, Stein variational inference, adversarial uncertainty estimation, or ensemble methods to produce error bars and assess confidence—particularly important for inverse problems and noisy data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse problems and parameter discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat unknown physical parameters γ as optimization variables jointly with network parameters θ to perform inverse modeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate loss to include data and residuals; include regularization and uncertainty quantification. Use same PINN framework for forward and inverse problems with minor modifications; ensure identifiability and careful weighting of data vs PDE residuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybridizing PINNs with classical numerical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine PINNs with numerical discretizations (FEM, finite volumes, finite differences) or with operator-learning methods for better performance or physical fidelity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numerical stencils inside CNNs, incorporate finite-volume discretization for conservation, or use FEM/variational embeddings. Hybrid approaches can leverage strengths of both data-driven and classical solvers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourier features and frequency-aware representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourier features, periodic activations, or spectral biases can help PINNs represent high-frequency components more effectively (mitigate frequency principle bias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sinusoidal activations or Fourier feature mappings to capture oscillatory solutions. Be aware of the frequency principle: standard networks tend to learn low frequencies first; use architectural or input feature engineering to accelerate high-frequency learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss norms and Sobolev / energy-based training
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of loss norm (L2, H1/Sobolev norms, energy norms) affects convergence properties and error control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider H1 or energy-norm-based losses when derivative accuracy or variational properties matter. Residual minimization in stronger norms can yield different approximation properties; choose according to PDE and desired error metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics and error estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess PINN performance via relative L2 errors, residual norms, convergence behavior, wall-clock time, and solution fidelity (e.g., conservation violations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report multiple metrics: relative error in solution norm, PDE residual distribution, boundary condition satisfaction, and computational cost. Use cross-validation, hold-out points, or analytical solutions for benchmarks. Consider error-estimation methods and theoretical bounds where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational cost, scalability, and distributed training
rubrics_metrics.description: PINNs can be computationally intensive (AD, large networks, many collocation points); scalability requires multi-GPU or distributed training frameworks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distributed training tools (e.g., Horovod), exploit parallel evaluation of collocation points, and design minibatch strategies. Balance collocation point count, network size, and optimizer choices to manage computational cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularization and handling noisy data
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularization (weight decay, dropout variants), robust loss choices, and Bayesian formulations help PINNs cope with noisy measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When training with noisy data, incorporate noise models (aleatoric/epistemic), use Bayesian PINNs, or include regularization terms. Robust loss functions and uncertainty quantification can prevent overfitting to noisy observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer learning and pretraining
rubrics_metrics.description: Pretraining a PINN or transferring parameters from related problems can speed convergence and improve generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pretrained networks as initializations across parametric sweeps or similar PDEs. Transfer learning can reduce required training iterations and help avoid poor local minima.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrete-time and time-stepping PINN variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrete time-stepping PINNs integrate temporal evolution using neural-network-based time integrators (e.g., using Runge–Kutta-like cells or recurrent architectures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For long-time integration or stiff temporal dynamics, use discrete-time schemes, recurrent PINN cells, or time-marching hybrid methods to improve stability and accuracy versus monolithic spatio-temporal training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural encoding of physical priors (hard constraints, symmetries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Embed physical structure (symmetries, conservation, boundary behavior) directly into network architecture or output parametrization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design networks that automatically satisfy invariances (e.g., equivariant layers), use multiplicative factors to impose BCs exactly, or build physics constraints into output parametrization to reduce search space and improve interpretability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of training data modalities (data-free vs data-assisted)
rubrics_metrics.description: PINNs can be trained purely from physics (data-free) or with a combination of physics and labeled data (data-assisted); the methodology differs accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For data-free settings rely on collocation/residual losses and BCs; for data-assisted or inverse problems include data-loss terms and model data noise. Balance physics and data via loss weights and consider multi-fidelity or multi-source data integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ensembles and model averaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensembles of PINNs can improve robustness and provide empirical uncertainty measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train multiple PINNs with varied initializations or architectures, aggregate predictions, and use ensemble spread as an uncertainty proxy. Ensembles help detect mode collapse or optimization failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring and diagnosing training (per-component losses, gradients, residual maps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Track individual loss components, gradient norms, and spatial residual distributions to diagnose failures and guide adaptive interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot PDE residual heatmaps, boundary residuals, gradient magnitudes per loss, and learning curves. Use diagnostics to trigger adaptive reweighting, resampling, or architecture modifications.
